title: Using ChatGPT for medical education: the technical perspective
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a ChatGPT-based chatbot can improve bedside history-taking education and facilitate international collaboration in medical training. The authors build on an earlier Dialogflow-based chatbot, Bennie and the Chats, which had limited flexibility, weak handling of unexpected questions, and high maintenance requirements. They ask whether a generative AI chatbot can provide a more natural, scalable, and adaptable simulated patient interaction for students.

The intervention is an improved version of the chatbot implemented with ChatGPT-3.5 Turbo through Azure OpenAI. Students act as physicians and converse with virtual patients whose cases are stored as de-identified JSON records and converted into prompts. The system also includes configurable patient personalities, multilingual interaction, profanity filtering, and an administrator interface for adding, editing, and deleting cases. The study was conducted as a cross-territory virtual bedside teaching activity co-hosted by the University of Hong Kong and the National University of Singapore.

A total of 70 undergraduate medical students and 13 patients participated, and 45 students completed an 11-point Likert questionnaire. Quantitative findings showed generally positive ratings for learning efficacy, learning experience, and the value of cross-university exposure, with strong positive correlations between usability-related ratings and overall learning outcomes. The qualitative comparison found that the ChatGPT version was simpler to maintain, better at handling irrelevant or multi-intent questions, and able to support multilingual, personality-based, and education-level variation. The paper concludes that ChatGPT-enabled virtual bedside teaching is a feasible supplementary tool for clinical history-taking education and could support broader international case sharing.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-method study using survey data and qualitative comparison, but it is not an RCT and lacks an objective achievement outcome or controlled causal design. The main evidence is self-reported perception and descriptive statistics, so only correlational/qualitative credibility is present.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and feasibility for a medical education chatbot, but it does not provide a measured learning gain effect size or strong causal evidence. Impact appears promising yet modest/unclear in terms of demonstrated educational achievement.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-powered virtual patient chatbot for bedside history-taking practice in medical education, using role-play prompts, patient personas, and multilingual conversation support.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports generally positive learning outcomes from a ChatGPT-based virtual bedside teaching system. Among 45 student survey respondents, the median rating for learning efficacy was 7/10 and 75.6% rated efficacy at 7 or above; the median for learning experience was 8/10 and 73.3% rated experience at 7 or above. This is a self-reported perception measure rather than an objective achievement test, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student Likert ratings of learning efficacy and overall learning experience in virtual bedside/history-taking teaching

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the chatbot supports clinical reasoning, communication, and history-taking practice through realistic patient dialogue, handling irrelevant and complex questions, and role-play with different personalities. Students rated interaction-related aspects positively (median 7/10; mean 6.64/10), but the evidence is based on perceptions and correlations rather than direct skill tests.
finding.measure: Student ratings of user-friendliness, keyword/input identification, interaction, and perceived learning effectiveness/experience

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable learning experience and engagement with the chatbot, and 73.3% rated the overall experience at 7 or above. The system design features such as different patient personalities and flexible multilingual interaction are presented as enhancing engagement, though the study does not directly measure motivation or persistence with validated instruments.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction/experience ratings and feedback on chatbot interaction

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that cross-territory virtual bedside teaching between HKU and NUS was feasible and perceived positively for international teaching collaboration. Among respondents, 82.2% agreed that exchanging patient cases helped them gain experience with diseases less prevalent in their own locality, suggesting institutional value for broader case sharing and collaboration.
finding.measure: Student agreement that international peer collaboration and case exchange improved learning outcomes/insights

finding.finding_summary: The technical comparison with the prior Dialogflow-based version indicates the ChatGPT system is simpler to develop and maintain, with lower maintenance cost and easier data updates by non-technical administrators. This is a qualitative assessment rather than a productivity experiment, so no numerical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of system design complexity, maintenance burden, and administrator usability
